newsitem.title: GERMANY: German debt rallies with T-bonds, looks vulnerable.
newsitem.headline: German debt rallies with T-bonds, looks vulnerable.

text.p: Bunds and futures rallied further in late European trade, boosted by gains in U.S. Treasuries, dealers said.
The German market appeared to unconcerned about domestic news from sources that the government expects a 20 billion shortfall in 1997 tax revenues. Official data are due for release on Thursday.

Traders said the apparent lack of concern in the Bund market was partly because the news was already priced in, and partly because players were waiting for details on what if any measures the government will take to make up the shortfall.
By 1437 GMT, the DTB June Bund future was trading 36 basis points higher on the day at 102.51, having spanned a price range of 102.01 to 102.57 so far in the session.
"Looking at the tax revenue news from an EMU-perspective, it decreases the chances of the whole thing going ahead," said Charles Diebel, senior fixed income analyst at Technical Data.
"Either it is going to be fudged or it is going to be delayed, but as yet it is not clear which way things will go."
Analysts say any moves to bluff EMU entry criteria will undermine confidence and increase downward pressure on Bunds and the mark, while delay would spark a rally in German assets.
For now, Bunds were happy to follow Treasuries higher, relying on the support of domestic fundamentals offering a long-term steady interest outlook, dealers said.
"The upmove in Bunds is more becuase there is little reason to sell, rather than because there are particular reasons to buy," said one.

But analysts said that with the June future flirting with levels as high as 102.50 this session -- bringing gains so far this week to almost 80 basis points -- overbought signals were starting to show through and could topple Bunds in the next few sessions if a spark comes from elsewhere.

In the cash market, the 10-year benchmark Bund was offering a yield of 5.68 percent at a price of 102.37 in late trade, while the yield spread to comparable U.S. paper had puffed out to 109 basis points from 107 at Tuesday's close.
Analysts said the market would continue to watch for budget and tax developments at home, while U.S. consumer price data for April would also attract attention abroad.
Analysts polled by Reuters are forecasting a slight fall in CPI in April, bringing the year-on-year rate down to 2.6 percent from 2.8 previously.
